qrdBas-a1270X-d1e101.summary: Rubric identifying the following as the single question on distinction 37 of Book 1.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e108.summary: States the question of the distinction: whether God is everywhere (ubique).

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e115.summary: First principal argument for the negative: Anselm (Monologion 22) holds that God is more properly said to be 'with' place and time than 'in' them, and is properly in no place or time; hence God is not everywhere or in all things.
claims: God is not properly said to be in any place or time.
Therefore God is not everywhere.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e135.summary: Second principal argument for the negative, from Augustine (83 Questions q.20): God is not 'somewhere' because all things are in him; if God were in all things, then, since all things are in God, all things would be in all things and God would be in himself, which is absurd.
claims: God is not anywhere because all things are in him.
If God were in all things, an absurd mutual containment would follow.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e145.summary: Third principal argument for the negative: what has nothing outside it is a whole; if God were (wholly) in one place he would be outside the other places, so he cannot be in a given place without being excluded from others.
claims: Being wholly in one place implies being outside others.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e152.summary: Fourth principal argument for the negative: if God is everywhere, he would change whenever a new place or thing comes to be, since he would then be where he was not before, as an angel is said to change by moving even without acquiring a new form.
claims: Omnipresence would entail divine change whenever a new place or creature arises.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e168.summary: Argument for the affirmative from Ambrose's De trinitate, cited in Lombard's text; the paragraph ends with the opening words of the author's plan ('First I will show that'), which continues in the next paragraph.
claims: God is everywhere, on Ambrose's authority.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e177.summary: First article of the plan (continuing the previous paragraph): to show that God is present everywhere and by what mode.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e184.summary: Second article of the plan: whether being everywhere is proper to God alone.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e189.summary: Third article of the plan: whether God's being everywhere and present to all things can be demonstrated from his omnipotence and immensity.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e199.summary: Opens the first article: since he has no demonstrative reasons, the author proceeds by authorities. Ambrose (De spiritu sancto I) proves the Holy Spirit is God and not a creature because he is everywhere, which is proper to God; so God is everywhere.
claims: God's omnipresence is established by authority rather than reason.
Being everywhere is proper to God, which shows the Holy Spirit is God.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e210.summary: Second authority: Augustine's letter to Dardanus says the Trinity cannot be hindered, since Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are in all places; hence God is everywhere.
claims: God is in every place.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e221.summary: Explains how God is everywhere, using Gregory's threefold scheme of essence, presence, and power. By essence God really penetrates and is intimate to all things (per the authorities). By presence, which here means seeing and knowing all things perfectly (as Elisha's 'was not my heart present?' indicates). By power, holding, conserving, governing, and producing all things (per Augustine, Literal Commentary on Genesis IV). The paragraph also notes special modes of presence (grace in saints, union in Christ's humanity, glory in the blessed) but sets them aside as off-topic.
claims: God is everywhere by essence, presence, and power.
Presence here means God's perfect cognition of all things.
Presence by power means conserving and governing all things, without which they would cease.
Special modes of indwelling (grace, union, glory) are distinct from general omnipresence.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e295.summary: Second article: specifies the precise sense in which being everywhere is proper to God. It means being in every place and thing that exists, as a singular thing, per se, and necessarily, so that God cannot fail to be in them while they exist, not through anything else or per accidens, and without any real relation to place. No creature has this.
claims: Being everywhere necessarily, per se, as a singular, and without a real relation to place is proper to God alone.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e299.summary: Draws consequences of the definition: a man would not be 'everywhere' in this sense even if he were the only being in the only place, and a universal is not everywhere in this way, since it is so only through singulars or merely by reason, being formally an ens rationis. Ends the second article and begins to report a view, completed in the next paragraph, that God's omnipresence can be demonstrated.
claims: Coextension with all actual place by accident does not satisfy the definition.
Universals are not everywhere in the proper sense, being everywhere only through singulars or in reason.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e330.summary: Third article: continues the report, begun at the end of the previous paragraph, of an opinion that God's real presence in all things can be demonstrated from divine omnipotence.
claims: Some hold that God's real omnipresence is demonstrable from omnipotence.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e339.summary: First argument for the opinion: by Physics VII every agent that moves something is really present to it (mover and moved are together); God acts on and conserves every thing and place immediately by omnipotence; so he is present to all.
claims: Every mover is really together with what it moves.
God immediately conserves and acts on everything, so he is present to everything.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e353.summary: Second argument for the opinion: nothing acts where it is not, especially when its action is its substance, as in God; God acts on every creature by producing or conserving it; so he is there. Confirmed by the case of the angel, which is said to be present where it operates and to be joined to a body by operation.
claims: Nothing acts where it is not, especially an agent whose action is its substance.
An angel is present where it operates, and likewise God.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e371.summary: Another argument for the opinion (labelled 'fourth'): a bodily agent acting immediately is present to and in contact with its patient, and would interpenetrate it if quantity did not prevent it; God, a non-quantitative agent acting immediately on everything, therefore makes himself intimate to everything.
claims: Immediate bodily agents touch their patients and would interpenetrate them but for quantity.
God, lacking quantity, is intimately present within all he acts on.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e412.summary: The author's position against the opinion: even granting that God's omnipotence (producing and conserving all things) were demonstrated, it does not evidently follow that God is everywhere; so he will argue against the opinion.
claims: God's omnipresence does not evidently follow from his omnipotence, even if omnipotence were demonstrated.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e400.summary: First argument against the opinion: the more powerful an agent, the more distant the thing it can act on; God is the most powerful agent, so his acting gives no proof of his real presence. Against the reply that powerful agents act at a distance only through intermediaries, the author argues that the sun heats some body first without heating the heavenly bodies in between, so it acts immediately on something to which it is not present. Illumination of the intermediaries is no counter, since light is not the principle of heating.
claims: Greater power allows action at greater distance.
The sun acts immediately (by heating) on something not present to it, without heating intermediaries.
So action does not prove presence.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e444.summary: Second argument against the opinion: on the opponent's own view the sun generates worms. Since no accident is the total ground for generating a substance and nothing less noble generates something more noble, the sun must act immediately on the matter, not through the surrounding air or water, and so acts on something to which it is not present. The paragraph also contains the third argument: even if the agent-presence reasoning proved anything, it would prove only that God assists the effect at a suitable proximity, as other agents do, not that he is intimately present within it.
claims: Spontaneous generation shows the sun acts immediately on distant matter.
An accident cannot be the total cause of a substance's generation.
The agent-presence argument would at most prove external proximity, not intimate presence.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e481.summary: Fourth argument against the opinion: an omnipotent agent acts by its will on whatever it wills, and the thing willed need not be present to the one willing. Objects moving an angel's intellect and will need not be present, nor need a speaking angel be present to its hearer; God's omnipotence is his will, so presence does not follow. Confirmed by creation: creating requires no prior presence or approximation, since creation precedes all presence, and the same seems to hold for conserving or moving creatures, as with creating and infusing grace or a soul. So the presence has not been demonstrated.
claims: Action by will does not require the presence of the willed object.
Creation presupposes no presence, and the same holds for conservation.
Hence God's presence is not demonstrated from his action.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e527.summary: The author's determination of the third article: that God is everywhere present by his immensity or immense essence is held by faith and the sayings of the saints alone, not from omnipotence or divine action on creatures. He cites Gregory's homily on the royal official and Lombard's text. Thought experiment: if God sat on one throne in heaven and were only there, he could still conserve and make everything and create an angel outside heaven, yet Scripture (Wisdom 8, Isaiah) says he is everywhere. The paragraph breaks off mid-sentence ('si illa propo-'), continued in the next.
claims: God's omnipresence by immensity is known by faith and authority alone.
A God localized in one place could still conserve and create all things, so action does not entail ubiquity.
Scripture teaches God's omnipresence.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e565.summary: Completes the sentence from the previous paragraph and replies to the first argument of the opinion: the principle that agent and patient must be together holds, if at all, only for corporeal agents acting through contrary qualities, not universally (as the sun case shows) and still less for God. Aristotle's arguments establish only that natural agents need some proximity to their patients, not presence.
claims: The mover-moved contact principle applies only to corporeal agents acting through contrary qualities.
Aristotle's arguments do not establish God's presence.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e596.summary: Reply to the second argument of the opinion: acting 'where' one is not differs from acting 'on' something to which one is not present. God need not be anywhere in order to act, as before creation. Alternatively, 'acting' named from the effect allows acting where one is not, while 'acting' named from the action (which is in God) does not. The reply that God acts where he is 'virtually' is rejected if virtual presence means God's power is really there, but accepted if it means only that his effect is there.
claims: God can act on what he is not present to.
Before creation God acted without being anywhere.
Virtual presence means only the presence of God's effect, not of God's power as really there.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e638.summary: Reply to the angelic confirmation: an angel need not be really present to the whole heaven to move it, since even philosophers with an undetermined motive intelligence do not put it in east and west at once; in any case the angelic case does not hold universally or for God, and something can operate on what it is not present to.
claims: An angel moves the whole heaven without being present to all of it.
The angelic analogy does not transfer to God.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e671.summary: Reply to the 'fourth' argument (on bodily agents' intimacy): it holds only for the natural agents Aristotle discusses, not for God. It also assumes falsely that an agent would interpenetrate its patient if it could; adequate assistance and approximation suffice, and the argument does not prove intimacy. Concludes the third article.
claims: The intimacy argument holds only for natural agents.
Agents do not tend to interpenetrate patients; assistance and approximation suffice.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e689.summary: Reply to the first principal argument (Anselm): God is not in place locally or in time temporally, as something measured or contained by them or bearing a real relation to them as creatures do. This is all Anselm means.
claims: God is not in place locally nor in time temporally.
God has no real relation to place or time.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e702.summary: Reply to the second principal argument (Augustine): Augustine means God is not in anything the way things are in him; God is somewhere not locally but presentially and really, and creatures are not in him that way. So the absurd mutual containment does not follow, since the two modes of 'being in' are not the same.
claims: God's being in things and things' being in God are different modes of inherence.
God is present really and presentially, not locally.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e721.summary: Reply to the third principal argument: God is wholly in one place in the sense that nothing of him is not there, not in the sense that he is not elsewhere, just as the soul is whole in the foot and whole in the hand.
claims: God is wholly in each place without being excluded from others.
The soul's whole presence in each bodily part is an analogy.

qrdBas-a1270X-d1e730.summary: Reply to the fourth principal argument: God does not change and has no real relation to place, as an angel does; his becoming newly present to a creature comes from the creature's change.
claims: God's new presence to new creatures involves change only in the creature.
God has no real relation to place.

qrdBas-a1270X.summary: Bassolis's single question on Book 1 d37 asks whether God is everywhere. Against four objections (from Anselm, Augustine, the logic of wholeness, and divine immutability), he proceeds in three articles. First, by authority (Ambrose, Augustine) rather than reason, God is everywhere, and in Gregory's three modes: by essence, by presence understood as perfect knowledge, and by power understood as conserving and governing. Second, being everywhere in the strict sense (as a singular, per se, necessarily, and without a real relation to place) is proper to God alone, not to a hypothetical lone human or to universals. Third, and most extensively, he rejects the opinion that God's real omnipresence can be demonstrated from omnipotence or divine action. Natural agents such as the sun act immediately on distant things, an omnipotent agent acting by will needs no presence to its object, creation presupposes no presence, and at most the argument would yield external assistance rather than intimacy. Omnipresence by immensity is therefore held by faith and the saints alone. He answers the opinion's arguments by restricting the Aristotelian contact principle to qualitative corporeal agents and by reading 'virtual presence' as presence of effect only, then resolves the initial objections by distinguishing modes of 'being in', using the soul-body analogy for total presence, and denying any real relation of God to place.
claims: God is everywhere by essence, presence (knowledge), and power.
Being everywhere per se, necessarily, as a singular, and without a real relation to place is proper to God alone.
God's omnipresence cannot be demonstrated from his omnipotence or action on creatures; it is held by faith and authority.
Agents, including natural ones like the sun, can act immediately on things to which they are not present.
God's new presence to new creatures implies no change in God, who has no real relation to place.
concepts: presence by essence, knowledge, and power
